name: Conventional dendritic cell
markers: CD8α (mouse marker for cDC1 in lymphoid organs)
summary: A professional antigen-presenting cell, recognised by its long branching arms. In tissues it samples its surroundings for antigen. Once it senses danger it matures and travels to a lymph node, where it shows peptides on MHC molecules and gives the co-stimulation naive T cells need. It is the main activator of naive T cells.
functions: Samples its surroundings in tissues such as skin, gut and lung by engulfing fluid and particles, and senses microbes with pattern-recognition receptors such as the Toll-like receptors.
Matures when it detects danger: it raises MHC molecules and the co-stimulators CD80 and CD86, makes cytokines such as IL-12, and switches on the chemokine receptor CCR7.

Travels to a lymph node: CCR7 guides it along CCL21 into lymphatic vessels and, in the afferent lymph, to the T-cell zone. Resident dendritic cells that come from the blood collect antigen draining into the node without travelling (shown mainly in mice).

Presents peptides on MHC class II to naive CD4 T cells and, by cross-presentation, peptides from outside antigens on MHC class I to naive CD8 T cells, together with co-stimulation. Cross-presentation is the speciality of the cDC1 subset.
Steers the fate of the T cells it activates through its cytokines: IL-12 favours Th1 cells, while other signals favour Th2, Th17, Tfh or regulatory T cells.
Helps other lymphocytes: it makes IL-12 and holds IL-15 on its surface to activate NK cells, and once licensed by CD40L from a helper T cell it activates CD8 T cells more strongly.
In its immature, steady-state form it presents self-antigens without co-stimulation, which helps keep T cells tolerant of the body's own tissues (shown mainly in mice).

Debated: how strictly the two main subsets divide the work (cDC1 for CD8 T cells and Th1, cDC2 for CD4 T cells and Th2 or Th17 responses), and how monocyte-derived dendritic cells that appear in inflammation should be grouped beside them. Single-cell studies keep splitting the human subsets.
abundance: Rare in blood: under 1% of white blood cells in adult humans, with cDC2 outnumbering cDC1 many times over. Most dendritic cells sit in tissues and lymphoid organs, not in blood. In mice they make up roughly 1% of spleen and lymph node cells.
